raw_response:
# Existing mechanisms for positional traversal of several sequences

I found five useful candidates. The strongest dated evidence is the 1 February 1999 Haskell report and a 26 June 1995 Standard ML basis draft. Other inspected pages are later revisions or have an uncertain publication date; they are retained as comparison evidence, without claiming they were available in the inspected form by 2000-08-03.

1. **Haskell 98 Prelude: zip, zip3, zipWith, and zipWith3.** [Original report, Standard Prelude](https://www.cse.iitb.ac.in/~as/fpcourse/haskell98_report/standard-prelude.html). These operations supply a clear, named mechanism for collecting corresponding elements into pairs or triples, or applying a function to each corresponding group, and stop when an input runs out. This directly informs the grouping operation and an explicit shortest-input rule. The [report title page](https://www.cse.iitb.ac.in/~as/fpcourse/haskell98_report/index.html) dates this version to 1 February 1999. Transfer caveat: Haskell lists and non-strict evaluation differ from Python's indexed sequence protocol; fixed-arity functions do not by themselves supply an arbitrary-arity interface.

2. **Standard ML ListPair, in the 1995 basis draft.** [A New Initial Basis for Standard ML](https://smlfamily.github.io/history/basis-1995-06-26.pdf), printed page 53 / PDF page 61. ListPair.zip forms pairs from matching positions and discards an unmatched tail, while ListPair.map and ListPair.app demonstrate separating tuple production from per-pair computation or effects. This helps keep the grouping primitive usable with an existing loop while allowing direct processing as a separate operation. The cover is dated 26 June 1995 and the ListPair page carries a 15 November 1994 last-change date. Transfer caveat: the interface handles two linked lists, so arbitrary arity and custom indexed objects require adaptation. For a mismatch-policy comparison, the [later rendered ListPair specification](https://smlfamily.github.io/Basis/list-pair.html) also documents zipEq and UnequalLengths; that inspected document was generated in April 2004, so I do not treat its strict variant as independently verified pre-cutoff evidence.

3. **SRFI 1's variadic zip and its public Scheme reference implementation.** [Specification](https://srfi.schemers.org/srfi-1/srfi-1.html) and [reference code](https://github.com/scheme-requests-for-implementation/srfi-1/blob/master/srfi-1-reference.scm). The specification groups one element from each of an arbitrary number of input lists into each output row, stopping at the shortest input, and the code implements the named wrapper by composing map with a list constructor. This is useful for both a discoverable public name and a compact arbitrary-arity implementation pattern. Transfer caveat: the implementation relies on Scheme list operations and the specified mapping semantics; a Python version must use its own sequence-access and exhaustion rules. The specification records final status on 9 October 1999 but also errata through October 2026; the exact inspected live code revision is undated, so I have not backdated that evidence.

4. **Common Lisp MAP over multiple sequences.** [HyperSpec MAP](https://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/f_map.htm). MAP applies a function to corresponding indexed elements from several sequences, with output length determined by the shortest sequence, providing a generalized sequence-level model rather than requiring a list-only API. This helps specify positional alignment and reuse a grouping operation across different sequence representations. Transfer caveat: Common Lisp's supported sequence types and explicit result-type/function arguments differ from Python's custom indexing objects, and the extra arguments do not alone solve the stated discoverability problem. The inspected live page has a 1996–2005 copyright range but no verified publication date for this revision, so its evidence date remains unknown.

5. **SGI STL binary transform and its input-iterator abstraction.** [SGI transform documentation mirror](https://www-f9.ijs.si/~matevz/docs/www.sgi.com/tech/stl/transform.html). Binary transform advances two input ranges together and applies an operation to each corresponding pair, showing how positional traversal can depend on an access abstraction instead of concrete container classes. This helps with the requirement to accommodate user-defined sequence representations. Transfer caveat: this algorithm takes the end of only the first input and requires the second range to be long enough; it is not a safe shortest-input policy without extra termination checks, and it directly combines values instead of exposing rows to an existing loop. The inspected mirror is not a dated release artifact; its footer includes 2001, and I leave the revision date unknown.

**Application to the supplied problem — inference from these mechanisms.** A named positional grouping operation can return ordinary rows for the existing loop to consume. Its adapter can request the same increasing index from every input, emit a row only when all required values are present, and end on the first ordinary exhaustion signal. That avoids requiring a separate length query from every custom sequence. The contract should state whether unmatched tails are discarded or a length mismatch is an error, distinguish ordinary exhaustion from unrelated access failures, and specify evaluation order when accessing inputs can have side effects. These are transfer suggestions, not claims of an existing Python implementation or proof of usefulness.

**Search and verification limits.** I used public web search and attempted the unauthenticated grep.app search endpoint; it was inaccessible through the available tool. The successful public-code inspection was a code-through-web fallback to the SRFI 1 repository, not native code-search success. An OCaml manual initially opened but subsequent attempts to read the relevant section timed out, so it was not promoted to a candidate. I did not retrieve or identify the target proposal, and observed no excluded-proposal references in the returned evidence. Model pretraining exposure remains uncontrolled.
